title: Gravitational potential of a planet — satellite orbit & escape energy

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: Gravitational potential is defined to be zero at infinity. The gravitational force is attractive, so work must be done on a mass to move it from a point in the field to infinity — the potential therefore rises towards zero from negative values, so near a point mass it is negative.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer:
φ = −GM/r, so M = −φr/G. From Fig. 1.1, at 1/r = 3.75×10⁻⁸ m⁻¹ the potential is φ = −2.2×10⁸ J kg⁻¹:
M = (2.2×10⁸/3.75×10⁻⁸)/6.67×10⁻¹¹ = 8.8×10²⁵ kg

title: Object on an oscillating platform — angular frequency & amplitude

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer:
Distance travelled per oscillation = 4x₀ → x₀ = 14×10⁻³/4 = 3.5×10⁻³ m
E = ½mω²x₀² → ω² = 2E/(mx₀²) = 2×2.2×10⁻⁴/(0.024×(3.5×10⁻³)²) = 1.50×10³
ω = 39 rad s⁻¹

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer:
The object loses contact when the maximum downward acceleration of the platform, ω²x₀, exceeds g:
x₀ = g/ω² = 9.81/39² = 6.4×10⁻³ m

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer: At the top of the oscillation — there the acceleration of the platform is a maximum downwards (a = −ω²x, magnitude ω²x₀). The object's maximum possible downward acceleration is g = 9.81 m s⁻², so it loses contact when ω²x₀ exceeds 9.81 m s⁻², i.e. first at the top of the oscillation.

title: Satellite in circular orbit — gravitational field strength & energy

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer:
The work done per unit mass
in bringing a small test mass from infinity to the point.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer: The gravitational potential is defined as zero at infinity. As the two masses move closer together (or as a mass is brought towards the planet), work is done by the gravitational field, so the potential falls below zero — hence it is negative.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer:
ϕ = −GM/r and, at X, −Φ = −GM/(4R), so GM/R = 4Φ.
At Y (radius R): potential = −4Φ

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.answer:
Since Φ = GM/(4R), GM = 4ΦR.
Field strength: g = GM/r²
X: g = GM/(4R)² = Φ/4R; Y: g = GM/R² = 4Φ/R
Potential energy: EP = −GMm/r
X: EP = −GM·M/4R = −MΦ; Y: EP = −GM·2M/R = −8MΦ

title: Resonance — damping & forced oscillations of a ball

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: Resonance is the phenomenon in which an oscillating system has its amplitude a maximum, and this occurs when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency of the system.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer: Light damping.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer: The oscillations of the ball lose energy because resistive forces (air resistance / friction in the string) act on the ball and do work against its motion, so the amplitude decreases gradually with time.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.answer:
Period T = 0.25 s (time between successive maxima of Fig. 4.2).
f = 1/T = 1/0.25 = 4.0 Hz

parts.label: (c)
parts.answer: A resonance curve: the amplitude rises from zero at f = 0, reaches a single maximum at f = 4.0 Hz (the natural frequency of the ball), and then falls again as f increases towards 10 Hz.

title: Disc with modelling clay — angular speed & centripetal acceleration

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: The angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc whose length is equal to the radius.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer: Draw an arrow labelled V from the modelling clay pointing in the NE direction — the velocity is tangential to the circular path (perpendicular to the radius of the disc).

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer: Draw an arrow labelled A from the modelling clay pointing in the NW direction, i.e. towards the centre of the disc (the direction of the centripetal acceleration).

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.answer:
Distance of the clay from the axis: r = 9.3 − 1.2 = 8.1 cm = 8.1×10⁻² m
v = rω
ω = v/r = 0.68 / 8.1×10⁻² = 8.4 rad s⁻¹

parts.label: (d)
parts.answer:
angular speed: same for both pieces — the disc is one rigid body, so every point has the same ω.
linear speed: less for the second piece — v = rω and the second piece is nearer the axis.
acceleration: less for the second piece — a = rω² and the second piece has the smaller radius.

title: Block oscillating on a spring — simple harmonic motion & energy

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: Fig. 4.2 is a straight line through the origin, showing that a is proportional to x; its negative gradient shows that a and x are always in opposite directions, i.e. a = −ω²x.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer:
a = −ω²x with x0 = 3Y and a_max = 2A:
2A = ω²(3Y)
ω = √(2A/3Y)

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.answer:
E = ½mω²x0² = ½m × (2A/3Y) × (3Y)²
= ½m × 6AY = 3mAY

parts.label: (c)
parts.answer:
ω = 2π/T = 2π/0.75 = 8.4 rad s⁻¹; amplitude x0 = 3Y = 1.8 cm
x = x0 sin ωt
x = 1.8 sin (8.4t) (x in cm, t in s)

title: Satellite in circular orbit — Newton's law & orbital period graph

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: The gravitational force between two point masses is directly proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them: F = Gm₁m₂/r².

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer: The gravitational force on the satellite acts towards the centre of the planet, so it is always perpendicular to the direction of motion of the satellite. This force provides the centripetal acceleration, so the satellite moves in a circular path at constant speed.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer:
Gravitational force = centripetal force:
GMm/(h + B)² = m(h + B)ω², with ω = 2π/T
GM/(h + B)² = (h + B)(2π/T)²
(h + B)³ = GMT²/4π² = (GA/4π²)T²
where A = M (the mass of the planet) and B = the radius of the planet.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.answer:
From Fig. 1.1, gradient m = (1280 − 360)/(12×10⁶) = 7.7×10⁻⁵ s²/³ m⁻¹.
Since T²/³ = m(h + B), the intercept is mB, and m³ = 4π²/GA.
A = 4π²/(Gm³) = 4π²/(6.67×10⁻¹¹ × (7.7×10⁻⁵)³) = 1.3×10²⁴ kg
B = intercept/m = 360/(7.7×10⁻⁵) = 4.7×10⁶ m

title: Block oscillating on a spring — amplitude, angular frequency & sketch

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: Motion in which the acceleration is directly proportional to the displacement from a fixed point (the equilibrium position) and is always directed towards that fixed point (opposite in direction to the displacement).

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer:
From Fig. 4.2, the turning points (v = 0) are at h = 3.5 cm and h = 9.5 cm.
amplitude = (9.5 − 3.5)/2 = 3.0 cm

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer:
vmax = v₀ = ωx₀ → ω = v₀/x₀
ω = 9.5/3.0 = 3.2 rad s⁻¹

parts.label: (b)(iv)
parts.answer: A sinusoidal curve starting at a minimum (h = 3.5 cm) at t = 0, since the block is released from rest at its lowest point. Three complete cycles from t = 0 to t = 6.0 s (period 2.0 s), with all peaks at h = 9.5 cm and all troughs at h = 3.5 cm.

title: Probe approaching the Sun — field strength, potential & luminosity

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: Gravitational field (strength) is the force per unit mass acting on a small test mass placed in the field.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.answer:
F = L/(4πx²), so x² = L/(4πF), and g = GM/x², so x² = GM/g.
Eliminating x²: GM/g = L/(4πF), giving g = 4πGMF/L.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.answer:
Read from Fig. 2.1 a consistent pair of values, e.g. F = 1.83×10³ W m⁻² when g = 8.0×10⁻³ N kg⁻¹.
L = 4πGMF/g = (4π × 6.67×10⁻¹¹ × 1.99×10³⁰ × 1.83×10³)/(8.0×10⁻³)
= 3.8×10²⁶ W

title: Pendulum in simple harmonic motion — energy & EK sketch

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: An arrow drawn from the centre of the sphere, perpendicular to the string, pointing left and down — the resultant (restoring) force is directed towards the equilibrium position.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer: amplitude = 0.016 m (maximum displacement, read from Fig. 5.2)

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer:
T = 0.40 s (from Fig. 5.2)
ω = 2π/T = 2π/0.40
= 16 rad s⁻¹

parts.label: (c)
parts.answer: A dome-shaped curve starting and ending on the x-axis at x = ±0.016 m, rising to a maximum of 4.7×10⁻³ J at x = 0 — kinetic energy is zero at the extremes of the oscillation and maximum at the equilibrium position.

title: Steel ball inside a hollow cone — circular motion & angular speed

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: An arrow vertically downwards labelled ‘weight’, and an arrow perpendicular to the cone surface, pointing inwards and upwards, labelled ‘normal contact force’ (the two arrows must be in the correct directions and correctly labelled).

parts.label: (b)
parts.answer: The vertical component of the contact force equals the weight, so there is no resultant force vertically. The horizontal component of the contact force is the resultant force, and it acts towards the centre of the circle — this provides the centripetal force that keeps the ball moving in a circle.

parts.label: (c)
parts.answer:
For a conical-pendulum type of motion the acceleration is a = g tan 52°, and a = v²/r:
9.81 × tan 52° = v²/0.15
v² = 0.15 × 9.81 × tan 52° = 1.88 m² s⁻²
v = 1.4 m s⁻¹

parts.label: (d)
parts.answer:
v = rω, so ω = v/r = 1.4/0.15
= 9.3 rad s⁻¹
(Equivalently ω = √(g tan 52°/0.15) = 9.3 rad s⁻¹.)

parts.label: (e)
parts.answer: The resultant (centripetal) force — hence the acceleration — is unchanged, and a = v²/r, so v² is proportional to r. Therefore increasing the speed requires a larger radius, so the ball moves up the cone to a circle of larger radius.

title: Gravitational potential of a planet & electric potential between plates

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: Sketch φ against x: a curve lying entirely in the negative-φ region for x between R and 4R, starting at (R, −φ) with a continuously decreasing magnitude and continuously decreasing gradient (concave up towards zero), and passing through (2R, −½φ) and (4R, −¼φ). The potential is φ = −GM/x, so it halves as x doubles.

parts.label: (b)
parts.answer: A geostationary satellite stays at the same point above the Earth, so its gravitational potential is constant: a horizontal straight line from t = 0 to t = 24 hours, starting at (0, −φ).

parts.label: (c)
parts.answer: The field between the plates is uniform, so the potential falls uniformly: a straight line with constant negative gradient from (0, V) to (d, 0), i.e. the potential decreases linearly from the positive plate to the negative plate.

title: Piezoelectric crystal — simple harmonic motion & ultrasound

parts.label: (d)(i)
parts.answer: Apply an alternating p.d. across the crystal. The p.d. causes the crystal to distort (change shape) at the frequency of the alternating p.d., so the surface vibrates — and conversely an oscillating crystal generates an alternating e.m.f., so it can be used to generate ultrasound.

parts.label: (d)(ii)
parts.answer:
Z = ρc, so Zmuscle = 1100 × 1600 = 1.76 × 10⁶ and Zbone = 1900 × 4100 = 7.79 × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹.
Intensity reflection coefficient = (Z₁ − Z₂)²/(Z₁ + Z₂)²
= (7.79 − 1.76)²/(7.79 + 1.76)² = 0.40 (40%)
so percentage transmitted = 60%

title: Gravitational potential & field of Mars — satellite orbit

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer:
The work done per unit mass
in moving a small test mass from infinity to the point.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer:
The satellite moves from r₁ = (3.4 + 1.7) × 10⁶ = 5.1 × 10⁶ m to r₂ = (3.4 + 6.8) × 10⁶ = 10.2 × 10⁶ m from the centre of Mars. Using ΔEP = GMm(1/r₁ − 1/r₂):
5.1 × 10⁸ = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × M × 122 × [(5.1 × 10⁶)⁻¹ − (10.2 × 10⁶)⁻¹]
M = 6.4 × 10²³ kg

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.answer: The satellite stays over the same point of Mars, so its period equals Mars’s rotation period: Mars takes (just under) 25 hours to rotate once on its axis.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.answer: The orbit is equatorial, and/or the satellite orbits in the same direction as the rotation of Mars.

title: Floating block — simple harmonic motion & energy

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.answer: The oscillation extends from h = 0.8 m to h = 2.0 m about the equilibrium at h = 1.4 m, so the amplitude = 0.60 m.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.answer: The line is a straight line through the origin, showing a ∝ −(displacement), so the oscillations are simple harmonic.

parts.label: (b)
parts.answer: Any three of: the mean/equilibrium position is at h = 1.4 m; the total energy of the oscillations is 9.0 J; the angular frequency is 1.2 rad s⁻¹ (period 5.1 s, or frequency 0.19 Hz); the maximum speed is 0.73 m s⁻¹; the mass of the block is 33 kg.

parts.label: (c)
parts.answer: A U-shaped curve resting on the h-axis (minimum at EP = 0), drawn between h = 0.8 m and h = 2.0 m with the minimum at h = 1.4 m and both end-points at EP = 9.0 J (since EP = total energy − EK).

title: Bicycle chain & cogs — radian, angular speed & period

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: The angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc whose length is equal to the radius.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer:
v = rω, so ω = v/r = 17/0.46
= 37 rad s⁻¹

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.answer:
distance moved = circumference of the small cog = 2πr = 2π × 0.038
= 0.24 m

parts.label: (b)(iv)
parts.answer:
angle = arc length/radius = 0.24/0.15
= 1.6 rad

parts.label: (c)
parts.answer: The rear wheel still rotates at the same angular speed (the bicycle speed is unchanged), but the rear cog is now smaller, so point X on the chain moves through a smaller distance in the same time — the linear speed of the chain decreases. The large cog (fixed to the pedals) has the same radius, so the angular speed of the pedals decreases.

title: Simple harmonic motion — displacement, velocity & phase

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: Motion in which the acceleration is (directly) proportional to the displacement and is always directed towards a fixed point (in the opposite direction to the displacement).

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer:
period = 2π/ω = 2π/16
= 0.39 s

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer:
v₀ = ωx₀, so x₀ = v₀/ω = 0.56/16
= 0.035 m

parts.label: (b)(iv)
parts.answer: A closed loop (ellipse) surrounding the origin, crossing the x-axis (v = 0) at x = ±3.5 cm and crossing the v-axis (x = 0) at v = ±0.56 m s⁻¹.

title: Gravitational potential & field of Mars — satellite orbit

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer:
The work done per unit mass
in moving a small test mass from infinity to the point.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer:
The satellite moves from r₁ = (3.4 + 1.7) × 10⁶ = 5.1 × 10⁶ m to r₂ = (3.4 + 6.8) × 10⁶ = 10.2 × 10⁶ m from the centre of Mars. Using ΔEP = GMm(1/r₁ − 1/r₂):
5.1 × 10⁸ = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × M × 122 × [(5.1 × 10⁶)⁻¹ − (10.2 × 10⁶)⁻¹]
M = 6.4 × 10²³ kg

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.answer: The satellite stays over the same point of Mars, so its period equals Mars’s rotation period: Mars takes (just under) 25 hours to rotate once on its axis.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.answer: The orbit is equatorial, and/or the satellite orbits in the same direction as the rotation of Mars.

title: Floating block — simple harmonic motion & energy

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.answer: The oscillation extends from h = 0.8 m to h = 2.0 m about the equilibrium at h = 1.4 m, so the amplitude = 0.60 m.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.answer: The line is a straight line through the origin, showing a ∝ −(displacement), so the oscillations are simple harmonic.

parts.label: (b)
parts.answer: Any three of: the mean/equilibrium position is at h = 1.4 m; the total energy of the oscillations is 9.0 J; the angular frequency is 1.2 rad s⁻¹ (period 5.1 s, or frequency 0.19 Hz); the maximum speed is 0.73 m s⁻¹; the mass of the block is 33 kg.

parts.label: (c)
parts.answer: A U-shaped curve resting on the h-axis (minimum at EP = 0), drawn between h = 0.8 m and h = 2.0 m with the minimum at h = 1.4 m and both end-points at EP = 9.0 J (since EP = total energy − EK).

title: Gravitational field & potential of the Earth

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: Gravitational field is the force per unit mass acting on a small test mass placed at the point.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer: The field lines are radial, pointing towards the centre of the planet.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer: For small changes in height, the change in height is very much smaller than the radius of the planet, so (R + h)² ≈ R² — the field lines are approximately parallel and g is approximately constant.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.answer:
At the surface g = GM/R², so 9.81 = 3.99 × 10¹⁴/R²
R = √(3.99 × 10¹⁴/9.81) = 6.38 × 10⁶ m

parts.label: (d)
parts.answer: The potential energy is zero at infinite separation, and the gravitational force is attractive — work is done by the field as the masses come together, so the potential energy falls below zero and is always negative.

title: Simple pendulum — frequency & maximum displacement

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: Motion in which the acceleration is (directly) proportional to the displacement and is always directed towards a fixed point (in the opposite direction to the displacement).

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer: The sphere passes through the equilibrium position in the same direction at t₁ and t₅ (or t₃ and t₇).

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer:
The interval t₁ → t₆ is 1.25 periods, so T = 2.2/1.25 = 1.76 s.
f = 1/T = 1.25/2.2 = 0.57 Hz

parts.label: (c)
parts.answer:
v₀ = ωx₀ with ω = 2πf, so x₀ = v₀/(2πf) = 0.080/(2π × 0.57)
= 0.022 m

title: Damped oscillations — magnet in a coil & electromagnetic induction

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.answer: Damping is the loss of energy from the oscillations due to resistive forces.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.answer: The amplitude of the oscillations decreases gradually (the oscillations continue for several periods).

parts.label: (a)(iii)
parts.answer: The oscillating magnet cuts magnetic flux, inducing an e.m.f. in the coil. This drives a current through the resistor, which dissipates thermal energy. By conservation of energy this thermal energy comes from the energy of the oscillations, so the oscillations are damped.

parts.label: (b)
parts.answer: For a given induced e.m.f. the current is smaller, so thermal energy is dissipated at a lower rate (the resistive force is smaller). The oscillations are therefore less damped — the amplitude decreases more slowly and they continue for longer.

title: Circular motion & simple harmonic motion — shadow projection

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: The velocity and acceleration both have constant magnitude, and the velocity is always perpendicular to the acceleration (the velocity is tangential and the acceleration is directed towards the centre).

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer: v = Rω

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer: a = Rω² = (Rω)ω = vω

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.answer: x = R sin θ

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.answer: θ = ωt

parts.label: (c)(iii)
parts.answer: Substituting θ = ωt into x = R sin θ gives x = R sin ωt.

parts.label: (c)(iv)
parts.answer: The equation is of the form x = x₀ sin ωt, the defining equation of simple harmonic motion (with amplitude x₀ = R), so the shadow's motion is simple harmonic.

parts.label: (d)(i)
parts.answer: amplitude = diameter/2 = 0.46/2 = 0.23 m

parts.label: (e)
parts.answer: The shadow is at the extreme of its motion — at the left-hand edge of the circular path (maximum displacement from P), labelled A, where the acceleration is a maximum.

title: Gravitational field — point masses & two spheres

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: The force per unit mass acting on a small test mass placed at the point.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer: F = GMm/x² and g = F/m, so g = [GMm/x²]/m = GM/x², where G is the gravitational constant.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer: An arrow at P pointing directly towards the point mass.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.answer: The field at Q is in the opposite direction to that at P (towards the mass), and is four times the field strength at P (Q is at distance x/2, and g ∝ 1/x²).

parts.label: (c)
parts.answer: A line starting at (R, −g₀) and ending at (L − R, +g₀), passing through (L/2, 0), becoming shallower from R to L/2 and steeper again from L/2 to L − R.

title: Circular motion of a student at latitude 52.2°

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer: An arrow pointing horizontally to the left (towards the Earth’s axis of rotation).

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.answer: An arrow downwards from the student (towards the centre of the Earth) labelled ‘weight’, and an upwards arrow (the normal contact force) pointing slightly to the left of the normal, labelled ‘contact force’ — their resultant is the horizontal centripetal force.

title: Simple harmonic motion & heavy damping — steel ball in oil

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.answer: The graph is a straight line through the origin, showing a is proportional to x, and its negative gradient shows a is always in the opposite direction to x — so the oscillations are simple harmonic.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.answer:
a₀ = ω²x₀ and ω = 2π/T, so T = 2π√(x₀/a₀) = 2π√(1.2/13)
= 1.9 s

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer: Damping is the loss of energy from the oscillations due to resistive forces.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer: A line starting at x = ±1.2 cm at t = 0 (entirely above or below the t-axis), with both the magnitude of x and the magnitude of the gradient continuously decreasing — heavy damping, so the ball returns to equilibrium without oscillating.

title: Circular motion & simple harmonic motion — shadow projection

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: The velocity and acceleration both have constant magnitude, and the velocity is always perpendicular to the acceleration (the velocity is tangential and the acceleration is directed towards the centre).

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer: v = Rω

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer: a = Rω² = (Rω)ω = vω

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.answer: x = R sin θ

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.answer: θ = ωt

parts.label: (c)(iii)
parts.answer: Substituting θ = ωt into x = R sin θ gives x = R sin ωt.

parts.label: (c)(iv)
parts.answer: The equation is of the form x = x₀ sin ωt, the defining equation of simple harmonic motion (with amplitude x₀ = R), so the shadow's motion is simple harmonic.

parts.label: (d)(i)
parts.answer: amplitude = diameter/2 = 0.46/2 = 0.23 m

parts.label: (e)
parts.answer: The shadow is at the extreme of its motion — at the left-hand edge of the circular path (maximum displacement from P), labelled A, where the acceleration is a maximum.

title: Gravitational field — point masses & two spheres

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: The force per unit mass acting on a small test mass placed at the point.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer: F = GMm/x² and g = F/m, so g = [GMm/x²]/m = GM/x², where G is the gravitational constant.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer: An arrow at P pointing directly towards the point mass.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.answer: The field at Q is in the opposite direction to that at P (towards the mass), and is four times the field strength at P (Q is at distance x/2, and g ∝ 1/x²).

parts.label: (c)
parts.answer: A line starting at (R, −g₀) and ending at (L − R, +g₀), passing through (L/2, 0), becoming shallower from R to L/2 and steeper again from L/2 to L − R.

title: Binary star — Newton’s law, orbit & centripetal acceleration

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: The gravitational force is (directly) proportional to the product of the two masses and inversely proportional to the square of their separation.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.answer:
a = rω² with ω = 2π/T. Since RB = 2RA and RA + RB = 3.3 × 10¹² m, RA = 3.3 × 10¹²/3 = 1.1 × 10¹² m.
T = 2π√(r/a) = 2π√(1.1 × 10¹²/1.2 × 10⁻⁵)
= 1.9 × 10⁹ s

parts.label: (b)(iv)
parts.answer: centripetal acceleration: B greater than A (a = F/m, and B has the smaller mass); linear speed: B greater than A (v = rω, and B has the larger radius); period: B equal to A (both orbit X with the same period).

title: Simple harmonic motion — frequency, energy & interchanges

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: The number of oscillations per unit time.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer: The kinetic energy reaches its maximum/minimum/zero twice in a cycle, so one complete cycle takes 0.80 s.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.answer: Any three of: the oscillations are simple harmonic; the amplitude = 0.016 m; the maximum speed = 0.13 m s⁻¹; the total energy = 7.0 × 10⁻⁴ J; the mass of the object = 0.087 kg; the maximum momentum = 0.011 kg m s⁻¹.

parts.label: (b)(iv)
parts.answer: The kinetic energy is a maximum at zero displacement and zero at maximum displacement, while the potential energy is zero at zero displacement and a maximum at maximum displacement. The sum of the kinetic and potential energies is constant (total energy).

title: Gravitational potential & field strength of a uniform planet

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer:
The work done per unit mass
in bringing a small test mass from infinity to the point.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer: The gravitational potential is defined as zero at infinity. Work is done by the two masses as they move towards each other (equivalently, work must be done on them to move them apart), so the potential decreases below zero — hence φ is negative for all values of x.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer:
ϕ = −GM/r. At the surface, r = R and ϕ = −Φ, so −Φ = −GM/R.
M = ΦR/G, where G is the (universal) gravitational constant.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.answer: g₀ = GM/R² = (ΦR)/R² = Φ/R

parts.label: (b)(iv)
parts.answer: Two curves: one in the top-left quadrant (between x = −3R and x = −R) and one in the bottom-right quadrant (between x = R and x = 3R). The upper curve passes through (−R, g₀) and (−2R, ¼g₀), with a non-zero value of g at x = −3R; the lower curve passes through (R, −g₀) and (2R, −¼g₀), with a non-zero value of g at x = 3R. Between −3R and −R the curve has a gradient and a magnitude of g that increase towards −R; between R and 3R the gradient and the magnitude of g decrease away from R. Nothing is drawn between x = −R and x = R.

title: Aircraft in horizontal circle — centripetal acceleration & banking angle

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: The acceleration is (always) perpendicular to the velocity, directed towards the centre of the circle, and the magnitudes of the velocity (the speed) and of the acceleration are constant — but their directions change continuously.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer: The only other force on the aircraft is its weight, which is vertical and has no horizontal component. The lift must therefore have a horizontal component (the resultant force towards the centre of the circle) to provide the centripetal force — so the lift cannot be vertically upwards.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer: Arrow drawn from the aircraft pointing horizontally to the left, i.e. towards the centre of the circle — the resultant force provides the centripetal force.

parts.label: (b)(iv)
parts.answer:
The vertical component of the lift balances the weight (L cos θ = mg) and the horizontal component of the lift causes the centripetal acceleration (L sin θ = ma):
tan θ = a/g = 4.5/9.81
θ = 25°

title: Earth's gravitational field — mass, potential & satellite energy

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.answer: The gravitational field (strength) at a point is the force per unit mass acting on a small test mass placed at that point.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.answer: Draw four straight, parallel field lines perpendicular to the ground (vertical), approximately evenly spaced, with arrows pointing downwards towards the ground.

title: Block oscillating on a spring — amplitude & kinetic energy

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.answer: The amplitude is the magnitude of the maximum displacement of the block from its equilibrium (mean) position.

parts.label: (b)
parts.answer: Sketch a dome-shaped curve, symmetrical about the EK-axis, with a single peak of 13 μJ at x = 0, falling to EK = 0 at x = ±8.4×10⁻³ m (the amplitude). Add a consistent x-axis scale with at least one marking in each half (e.g. ±8 and ±4, in units of 10⁻³ m), corresponding to the end points.

title: Gravitational potential & field strength of a uniform planet

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: The gravitational potential at a point is the work done per unit mass in bringing a small test mass from infinity to that point.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer:
The potential is defined as zero at infinity.
Work is done by the two masses as they move towards each other from infinity (or work must be done on them to increase their separation), so their gravitational potential energy decreases — hence the potential at any finite point is negative for all values of x.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer:
At the surface: ϕ = −GM/R = −Φ
M = ΦR/G, where G is the universal gravitational constant.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.answer: g0 = GM/R² = G(ΦR/G)/R² = Φ/R

parts.label: (b)(iv)
parts.answer:
Draw two curves — one in the top-left quadrant and one in the bottom-right quadrant (nothing drawn between x = −R and x = +R).
Each curve must pass through (±R, ±g0) and (±2R, ±¼g0), with a non-zero value of g at ±3R.
The magnitudes of both g and the gradient decrease as |x| increases (g ∝ 1/x²), so each curve flattens towards the x-axis away from the planet.

title: Geostationary satellite — Earth's mass & mean density

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.answer: A geostationary orbit is one in which the satellite remains above the same point on the Earth's surface.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.answer: Any two of: the orbit is equatorial (directly above the Equator); the satellite orbits from west to east; the orbital period is 24 hours (equal to the Earth's period of rotation).

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer: v = 2πR/T

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer:
GMm/R² = mRω² and ω = 2π/T:
GMm/R² = mR(2π/T)² → M = 4π²R³/(GT²)

title: Ball on a spring — velocity–displacement graph & resonance

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.answer: Draw a smooth closed loop (ellipse) enclosing the origin, cutting the x-axis at x = ±2.5 cm (and nowhere further out) and the v-axis at v = ±4.4 cm s⁻¹ (and nowhere further out). The v–x graph for s.h.m. is an ellipse, v = ±ω√(x₀²−x²), not straight lines between the intercepts.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer: Resonance is the oscillation of an object at maximum amplitude, which occurs when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency of the oscillating system.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer: Draw a curve rising continuously from f = 0 (amplitude never zero when f > 0) to a single peak at f = 0.28 Hz, then falling continuously to f = 0.40 Hz.
